title: HEALING BETWEEN STILLNESS AND SPEECH
subtitle: A Reflection on Human Connection
author: Rishitha Gorupati

paragraphs: I’ve often wondered why understanding each other feels so complex. Why, in the moments we need each other the most, we seem to drift in different directions. When pain arrives, some need attention, while others need space. Some want to speak, while others want to stay quiet.
Ladies and gentlemen, you are completely different planets—yet close to each other. Not in distance, but in the way you feel, in the way you heal.
Life of Stillness
Can I say men are simple?
Yes, sometimes they are.

They are often goal-oriented, specific, and stubborn. They constantly try to prove to themselves that they can do it. They are often inclined towards technology, sports, adventure, and similar pursuits. They are often more interested in objects and things than in people and feelings.
Achieving goals is very important to a man because it is a way to prove himself, to prove his competence, and to feel good about himself.
Am I right, gentlemen?

But when it comes to relationships, when they get hurt, they often choose to withdraw from others and process things internally. They need space to regain clarity. They find healing in stillness. They go into their own space, reflecting on the cause of the problem and trying to find solutions. If they do not find a solution, they may divert themselves by engaging in other activities like watching television or gaming.

At that time, they prefer to be alone to heal from the pain. And it does not mean that they are ignoring or not giving attention to their partner. During this phase, offering unsolicited advice may not be beneficial, as it can make them feel incapable or that their competence is being questioned.
Life of Speech
Women may seem complicated, yet they are simple too.

They have different values. They love communicating with people. They nurture each other by sharing feelings and emotions. They do not always prefer uniformity like men. Communication is of primary importance to them.
Women are relationship-oriented. They often try to improve a man, but he may feel that she is trying to fix him. Here, one thing to remember is: don’t fix it unless it is broken.
Am I right, ladies?

When a woman gets hurt, she often finds healing by sharing her problems with her partner, friends, or family. At that moment, she does not seek advice or solutions. She simply needs 
her partner to be by her side and listen to her.
And in doing so, she begins to heal on her own. Sometimes, all she needs is a shoulder to share the pain she is going through—not a solution, but understanding.
Where Does the Conflict Start?

Until now, we have understood these two different worlds. But people often struggle because they fail to understand the opposite gender properly and assume that the other person will 
react and understand things the same way they do.
But is that not just an assumption? Let’s pause for a moment and consider an example.

A couple working in an IT company had a very hectic and stressful day. After coming back home, the man wanted some private time for himself to relax and heal, while the woman wanted to talk about how her day went so that she could feel relieved.

Here, the conflict begins—not because one is wrong, but because they fail to understand each other. Both people are right from their own perspectives, but when it comes to relationships, understanding each other plays a major role in avoiding conflicts.
So, how can this be resolved?
The Understanding

The solution, perhaps, does not lie in choosing silence over words, or words over silence—but in learning the timing of both. Maybe in that moment, it is not about who is right, but about what the other person needs.

A little space, given with understanding, does not mean disconnection—it allows connection to find its way back. And a conversation, received with patience, is not pressure—it is an attempt to feel less alone.

When he learns to say, “Give me some time, I’ll come back,” and when she learns to wait without feeling distant, something shifts. Silence no longer feels like absence, and words no longer feel overwhelming. Instead, they begin to meet somewhere in between—where healing becomes mutual, not individual.
Conclusion
Maybe, in the end, it was never about who was right, but about understanding what lies between silence and speech—where a quiet understanding waits.

When a man and a woman are able to respect and accept their differences, love is given a chance to blossom. And perhaps, when our partner resists us, it is not rejection, but a reflection of a mismatch in timing or approach.

Understanding these differences can make relationships healthier and more supportive.
If you are a woman, whenever your partner is upset or hurt, give him the space he needs. Let him heal in his own way, and avoid offering advice in that moment. His silence is not ignorance or lack of attention—it is simply his way of finding his way back to himself.

And if you are a man, be a patient listener for your partner. Offer your presence, your attention, and your understanding. She may not be looking for solutions, but for someone who truly hears her. Sometimes, all she needs is your support, your empathy, and a space where her words can rest.
Not all men withdraw, and not all women express—but many of us are shaped this way.
Some heal in silence, some in words—and understanding both is where love quietly begins.

concludingReflection: Some heal in silence, some in words—and understanding both is where love quietly begins.
